days.title: The Cell Theory — Historical Development and Postulates
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Trace the historical development of the cell theory.
  • State the three postulates of the cell theory.
  • Explain how each postulate is supported by evidence.
  • Appreciate how technological advances in microscopy enabled the discovery of the cell.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cell — the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.
  • Cell Theory — the foundational principle stating that all living things are made of cells.
  • Microscopy — the technology that made cell discovery possible.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Before the Cell — A Quick Look Back

Before the 1600s, people believed that life could arise spontaneously from non-living matter (spontaneous generation). This changed when the microscope was invented.

B. The Scientists Behind the Cell Theory

YearScientistContribution
1665Robert HookeObserved cork; called the tiny compartments "cells"
1674Anton van LeeuwenhoekFirst to observe living cells
1831Robert BrownDiscovered the nucleus
1838Matthias SchleidenAll plants are made of cells
1839Theodor SchwannAll animals are made of cells
1855Rudolf VirchowCells arise only from pre-existing cells

C. The Three Postulates

  1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
  2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living organisms.
  3. All cells arise from pre-existing cells.

D. Modern Additions

  • Cells contain hereditary information (DNA).
  • All cells have similar chemical composition.
  • Cell activity depends on subcellular structures.

💬 Let's Discuss

Imagine living in the 1600s: no one had ever seen anything smaller than a grain of sand, so it made sense to believe that maggots simply "appeared" in rotting meat. The cell theory did not come from one genius on one day. It was built over almost 200 years, and every step depended on a better lens.

When Robert Hooke looked at cork in 1665, he saw empty boxes — the walls of dead plant cells — and named them cells. A few years later Anton van Leeuwenhoek, using his own powerful single-lens microscopes, saw something Hooke never did: living cells swimming in pond water and saliva. For more than a century after that, the idea stayed a collection of observations. Only in 1838–1839 did Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) make the bold general claim that all organisms are made of cells. Notice what they still lacked: an explanation of where new cells come from. Schleiden actually thought cells crystallized out of fluid! In 1855 Rudolf Virchow completed the theory with omnis cellula e cellula — every cell comes from a pre-existing cell.

Why does this matter to you? The third postulate explains everyday events: a wound heals because skin cells divide, and you grew from one fertilized egg. It also ended the idea of spontaneous generation, which Louis Pasteur later disproved by experiment.

Common mistake: saying Hooke discovered living cells. He saw only the empty walls of dead cork cells. A good way to remember the order is see → claim → explain: first scientists saw cells, then they claimed all living things have them, and finally they explained where cells come from.

pairs.why: Hooke saw empty cork compartments that reminded him of small rooms (cellulae).
Leeuwenhoek's lenses let him see moving "animalcules" — the first living cells observed.
Brown described the dark central body in orchid cells — the nucleus.

pairs.right: All plants are made of cells
pairs.why: Schleiden studied plant tissues and concluded all plants are made of cells.

pairs.right: All animals are made of cells
pairs.why: Schwann extended the same idea to animal tissues.
Virchow's "omnis cellula e cellula" completed the theory: cells come only from cells.

scenarios.text: A scientist observes bacteria under a microscope — a single cell performing all life functions.
scenarios.explanation: One bacterial cell carries out every life function, so the cell is the basic unit of structure and function (Postulate 2).

scenarios.text: A cut heals because skin cells divide to replace damaged ones.
scenarios.explanation: Healing happens because existing skin cells divide to make new ones — cells come from pre-existing cells (Postulate 3).

scenarios.text: A leaf, a root, and a stem are all made of microscopic units.
scenarios.explanation: Leaf, root and stem tissues are all built from cells, so the plant is composed of cells (Postulate 1).

scenarios.text: A fertilized egg divides repeatedly to form an embryo.
scenarios.explanation: Every cell of the embryo comes from division of the zygote — cells arise from pre-existing cells (Postulate 3).

scenarios.text: Every organism studied — from fungi to whales — is made of cells.
scenarios.explanation: Finding cells in every organism studied is direct support for 'all living things are made of cells' (Postulate 1).

scenarios.text: A cell's mitochondria produce energy for the cell's activities.
scenarios.explanation: Mitochondria work inside the cell to power its functions, showing the cell is the functional unit (Postulate 2).

questions.text: Who first coined the term "cell," and what was he observing?
questions.explanation: Hooke named the 'cells' he saw in thin slices of cork; Leeuwenhoek later saw living cells.

questions.text: Which postulate was added LAST, and who proposed it?
questions.explanation: Virchow added the third postulate in 1855, about 17 years after Schleiden and Schwann's work.

questions.text: Why was the invention of the microscope important to the cell theory?

choices.label: It let scientists see cells for the first time
It made cells grow larger in the laboratory
It proved that spontaneous generation is true
It removed the need for doing any experiments

questions.explanation: Cells are too small to see with the naked eye; the microscope let scientists observe them for the first time.

takeaways: The cell theory is the foundation of biology.
It was developed over ~200 years by multiple scientists.
Three postulates: all organisms are made of cells; cells are the basic unit of life; cells come from pre-existing cells.

days.title: The Plasma Membrane & Cytoplasm
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure of the plasma membrane using the fluid mosaic model.
  • Explain the functions of the plasma membrane.
  • Describe the composition and roles of the cytoplasm and cytosol.
  • Relate membrane structure to its selective permeability.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Plasma membrane — a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer that surrounds the cell.
  • Fluid mosaic model — describes the membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins.
  • Cytoplasm — the material within the cell, excluding the nucleus.
  • Cytosol — the liquid portion of the cytoplasm.

📚 Lesson Content

A. The Plasma Membrane — Structure

The plasma membrane follows the fluid mosaic model proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972).

ComponentDescriptionFunction
Phospholipid bilayerTwo layers of phospholipids with hydrophilic heads outward, hydrophobic tails inwardForms the basic barrier
Integral proteinsEmbedded within the bilayerTransport, channels, receptors
Peripheral proteinsAttached to the surfaceSignaling, structural support
CholesterolWedged between phospholipidsRegulates membrane fluidity
Glycolipids / GlycoproteinsCarbohydrate chains on outer surfaceCell recognition, adhesion

B. Functions of the Plasma Membrane

  • Selective permeability — allows some substances in, keeps others out.
  • Cell signaling — receptors detect chemical messages.
  • Cell recognition — identifies the cell as "self."
  • Anchoring — connects to cytoskeleton and other cells.

C. The Cytoplasm

  • Cytosol — the jelly-like fluid (mostly water, ions, enzymes)
  • Organelles — membrane-bound and non-membrane-bound structures
  • Cytoskeleton — protein filaments providing shape and movement
  • Inclusions — stored nutrients, pigments, crystals

D. Fluid Mosaic Model — Why "Fluid"?

Phospholipids and proteins can move laterally within the membrane. Fluidity is essential for cell movement, protein function, and membrane fusion.

💬 Let's Discuss

Every cell needs a border that is strong enough to hold its contents in but smart enough to let the right things through. That border is the plasma membrane, and the best description of it is the fluid mosaic model.

Picture a crowded swimming pool. The water surface is the phospholipid bilayer: each phospholipid has a water-loving (hydrophilic) phosphate head and two water-fearing (hydrophobic) fatty-acid tails. In water, they arrange themselves into two layers with the tails hidden in the middle. The swimmers floating around are the proteins. Some go all the way through the bilayer (integral proteins, used as channels and pumps); others sit on the surface (peripheral proteins, used for signaling and support). Because the parts can drift sideways, the membrane is fluid; because it is made of many different pieces, it is a mosaic.

Cholesterol acts like a buffer for fluidity: in warm conditions it keeps the membrane from becoming too runny, and in cold conditions it keeps it from becoming stiff. Sugar chains attached to lipids and proteins (glycolipids and glycoproteins) act like ID cards — this is how your immune system tells "self" from "non-self," and it is the basis of ABO blood types.

Because small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) slip through the tails easily but ions and large polar molecules cannot, the membrane is selectively permeable.

Common mistake: mixing up cytoplasm and cytosol. Cytoplasm is everything between the membrane and the nucleus, organelles included. Cytosol is only the jelly-like fluid part.

pairs.why: The double layer of phospholipids is the basic barrier — its hydrophobic core blocks ions and polar molecules.
Integral proteins span the bilayer, so they can form channels and carriers.
Peripheral proteins sit on the surface and help in signaling and anchoring the cytoskeleton.
Cholesterol sits between phospholipids and buffers fluidity in both heat and cold.
Sugar chains on the outer surface act as identification tags for cell recognition.
Cytosol is the fluid part of the cytoplasm where organelles are suspended.

scenarios.text: A scientist notices that membrane proteins drift laterally within the bilayer.
scenarios.explanation: Lateral drifting of proteins is exactly what 'fluid' means in the fluid mosaic model.

scenarios.text: Chains of sugars on the outer surface identify the cell as "self."
scenarios.explanation: Glycoproteins carry sugar chains that mark the cell as 'self'.

scenarios.text: A molecule moves from outside to inside without using energy.
scenarios.explanation: Movement down a concentration gradient without ATP is passive transport.

scenarios.text: Cholesterol keeps the membrane from becoming too rigid or too fluid.
scenarios.explanation: Cholesterol prevents extremes — this is fluidity regulation.

scenarios.text: The plasma membrane lets K⁺ in but blocks Na⁺.
scenarios.explanation: Letting one ion in while blocking another shows the membrane chooses what passes: selective permeability.

scenarios.text: Everything inside the cell except the nucleus.
scenarios.explanation: Cytoplasm includes cytosol and organelles — everything inside except the nucleus.

questions.text: Which model describes the plasma membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins?
questions.explanation: The fluid mosaic model (Singer & Nicolson, 1972) pictures moving proteins in a fluid lipid bilayer.

questions.text: What is the primary function of cholesterol in the plasma membrane?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol keeps the membrane from being too fluid when warm and too rigid when cold.

questions.text: What is the difference between cytoplasm and cytosol?

choices.label: They are two names for exactly the same thing
Cytoplasm includes organelles; cytosol is only fluid
Cytosol includes the organelles; cytoplasm does not
Cytoplasm is found only inside plant cells

questions.explanation: Cytoplasm = cytosol + organelles (outside the nucleus); cytosol is only the fluid part.

takeaways: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins (fluid mosaic model).
It is selectively permeable, controlling what enters and exits the cell.
The cytoplasm includes cytosol, organelles, and the cytoskeleton.
Membrane fluidity is essential for cell function.

days.title: Major Organelles — Nucleus, Ribosomes, ER
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure and function of the nucleus.
  • Explain the roles of ribosomes in protein synthesis.
  • Differentiate rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
  • Explain how the endomembrane system works together.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Nucleus — the control center of the cell containing DNA.
  • Ribosome — the site of protein synthesis.
  • Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) — a network of membranes for synthesis and transport.
  • Endomembrane system — ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vesicles working together.

📚 Lesson Content

A. The Nucleus

StructureFunction
Nuclear envelope (double membrane)Separates nucleus from cytoplasm
Nuclear poresAllow exchange of materials (mRNA, proteins)
NucleolusSite of ribosome assembly
ChromatinDNA + proteins (chromosomes when condensed)
NucleoplasmJelly-like fluid inside the nucleus

B. Ribosomes

  • Structure: Two subunits (large + small), made of rRNA and proteins
  • Function: Protein synthesis (translation)
  • Types: Free ribosomes (internal proteins) vs. Bound ribosomes (proteins for export)
  • Found in: Both prokaryotes (70S) and eukaryotes (80S)

C. Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)

TypeStructureFunction
Rough ERStudded with ribosomesProtein synthesis, folding, and transport
Smooth ERNo ribosomes; tubularLipid synthesis, detoxification, calcium storage

D. The Endomembrane System

  1. Ribosome → protein synthesized into rough ER
  2. Rough ER → protein folded and modified
  3. Vesicle → carries protein to Golgi apparatus
  4. Golgi → further modifies, sorts, and packages
  5. Vesicle → delivers to destination

💬 Let's Discuss

Think of a cell as a factory that makes proteins. The nucleus is the main office where the master plans (DNA) are kept. The plans never leave the office; instead, copies called mRNA exit through the nuclear pores in the double-layered nuclear envelope. Inside the nucleus, the nucleolus is the workshop that assembles ribosome subunits. DNA in a non-dividing cell is loose and wrapped around proteins — this is called chromatin.

Ribosomes are the machines that read mRNA and link amino acids into proteins. Where a ribosome works determines where its protein goes. Free ribosomes in the cytosol make proteins that stay inside the cell (for example, enzymes of glycolysis). Bound ribosomes attached to the ER make proteins that will be exported, placed in membranes, or sent to lysosomes.

The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membranes continuous with the nuclear envelope. The rough ER is studded with ribosomes; newly made proteins enter its interior, where they are folded and often tagged with sugars. The smooth ER has no ribosomes and does other jobs: making lipids such as phospholipids and steroid hormones, storing calcium in muscle cells, and detoxifying drugs and alcohol — which is why liver cells are full of smooth ER.

So the protein "assembly line" runs: ribosome → rough ER → (vesicle) → Golgi → vesicle → destination. Pancreas cells that export digestive enzymes have huge amounts of rough ER.

Common mistake: thinking the nucleolus is a separate organelle with its own membrane. It is only a dense region inside the nucleus.

pairs.why: The double nuclear envelope separates DNA from the cytoplasm.
Nuclear pores let mRNA and ribosome subunits out and proteins in.
The nucleolus makes rRNA and assembles ribosome subunits.
Chromatin is DNA wound around histone proteins.
Free ribosomes release their proteins into the cytosol, for use inside the cell.
Bound ribosomes send their proteins into the ER for export or for membranes.
Rough ER receives new proteins and folds and modifies them.
Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and makes lipids and detoxifies chemicals.

scenarios.text: A liver cell detoxifies alcohol after a night out.
scenarios.explanation: Detoxification of alcohol and drugs is a smooth ER job; liver cells have lots of it.

scenarios.text: A cell produces a lot of digestive enzymes for export.
scenarios.explanation: Exported enzymes are made on bound ribosomes and processed in the rough ER.

scenarios.text: A cell is building new ribosomes.
scenarios.explanation: Ribosome subunits are assembled in the nucleolus.

scenarios.text: mRNA exits the nucleus to reach ribosomes.
scenarios.explanation: mRNA leaves the nucleus through nuclear pores.

scenarios.text: A protein is folded into its 3D shape after synthesis.
scenarios.explanation: Newly made proteins enter the rough ER, where they are folded.

scenarios.text: A cell needs to synthesize new membrane phospholipids.
scenarios.explanation: Phospholipids are lipids, and lipid synthesis happens in the smooth ER.

questions.text: Which organelle is the site of ribosome assembly?
questions.explanation: The nucleolus makes rRNA and assembles ribosome subunits.

questions.text: What is the main difference between rough and smooth ER?

choices.label: Rough ER has ribosomes; smooth ER does not
Smooth ER is found only in plants
Rough ER makes lipids; smooth ER makes proteins

questions.explanation: The 'rough' look comes from attached ribosomes; smooth ER has none and makes lipids instead.

questions.text: Which sequence correctly describes the endomembrane system?
questions.explanation: Proteins are made on ribosomes, enter the rough ER, then go to the Golgi and leave in vesicles.

takeaways: The nucleus houses DNA and controls cell activities.
Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.
Rough ER handles proteins; smooth ER handles lipids and detoxification.
The endomembrane system coordinates synthesis, modification, and transport.

days.title: Energy & Support Organelles — Mitochondria, Chloroplasts, Cytoskeleton
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure and function of mitochondria.
  • Describe the structure and function of chloroplasts.
  • Explain the roles of the cytoskeleton in cell shape and movement.
  • Compare energy-related organelles in plant and animal cells.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Mitochondrion — the powerhouse of the cell (ATP production).
  • Chloroplast — site of photosynthesis in plant cells.
  • Cytoskeleton — network of protein filaments for shape, support, and movement.
  • Endosymbiotic theory — mitochondria and chloroplasts originated from engulfed prokaryotes.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Mitochondria — The Powerhouse

  • Structure: Double membrane; inner membrane folded into cristae; interior called matrix
  • Function: Cellular respiration — produces ATP
  • Contains: Its own DNA (mtDNA) and ribosomes
  • Found in: Both plant and animal cells

B. Chloroplasts — Site of Photosynthesis

StructureFunction
Outer & inner membraneEnclose the organelle
ThylakoidsMembrane sacs containing chlorophyll
GranaStacks of thylakoids (light reactions)
StromaFluid surrounding thylakoids (Calvin cycle)

C. The Cytoskeleton

ComponentStructureFunction
MicrofilamentsThin (actin)Cell shape, movement, muscle contraction
Intermediate filamentsMediumMechanical support, anchor organelles
MicrotubulesThick (tubulin)Spindle fibers, cilia, flagella, transport

D. Endosymbiotic Theory

Mitochondria and chloroplasts likely originated from ancient prokaryotes engulfed by a host cell. Evidence: own circular DNA, own 70S ribosomes, reproduce by binary fission, double membranes.

💬 Let's Discuss

A cell that works hard needs power and a strong framework. Mitochondria are the power plants: they carry out cellular respiration and turn the energy in glucose into ATP. The inner membrane is folded into cristae, which give more surface area for the electron transport chain — more folds, more ATP. The fluid inside, the matrix, is where the Krebs cycle happens. This is why heart and leg muscle cells contain hundreds to thousands of mitochondria.

Chloroplasts, found in plants and algae, capture light energy. Their internal membranes form flattened sacs called thylakoids, which contain chlorophyll and are stacked into grana. The surrounding fluid, the stroma, is where sugar is built in the Calvin cycle. Notice the partnership: chloroplasts make glucose and O₂; mitochondria (present in plant cells too!) use them to make ATP.

Both organelles have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes like bacteria, and double membranes, and they divide by a fission-like process. These clues support the endosymbiotic theory: long ago, a larger cell engulfed bacteria that became mitochondria and chloroplasts instead of being digested.

The cytoskeleton gives shape and movement. Microfilaments (actin) help muscle contraction and the pinching of cells during division. Intermediate filaments resist pulling forces, like steel cables. Microtubules are hollow tubes that form spindle fibers, cilia and flagella, and act as tracks for vesicles.

Common mistake: thinking plant cells have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria. Plant cells have both.

pairs.why: Cristae are folds of the inner membrane that increase surface area for ATP production.
The matrix is the fluid inside the inner membrane where the Krebs cycle happens.
Thylakoid membranes hold chlorophyll and the light reactions.
Grana are stacks of thylakoids, like piles of coins.
The stroma surrounds the thylakoids; the Calvin cycle happens there.
Actin microfilaments help the cell change shape and move.
Intermediate filaments are rope-like and resist tension.
Microtubules form the spindle, cilia and flagella.

scenarios.text: A muscle cell needs huge amounts of ATP.
scenarios.explanation: ATP is produced mostly in mitochondria through cellular respiration.

scenarios.text: A leaf cell captures sunlight to make glucose.
scenarios.explanation: Chloroplasts capture light and make glucose by photosynthesis.

scenarios.text: A cell divides and needs spindle fibers.
scenarios.explanation: Spindle fibers that pull chromosomes apart are made of microtubules.

scenarios.text: A cell moves using a flagellum.
scenarios.explanation: Flagella are built from microtubules in a 9+2 arrangement.

scenarios.text: A scientist finds circular DNA and 70S ribosomes in an organelle.
scenarios.explanation: Circular DNA and 70S ribosomes resemble bacteria — evidence for endosymbiosis.

scenarios.text: An organelle has stacked membranes filled with chlorophyll.
scenarios.explanation: Stacked chlorophyll-filled membranes are the grana of a chloroplast.

questions.text: What is the main function of mitochondria?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria produce most of the cell's ATP through cellular respiration.

questions.text: Which structure inside the chloroplast contains chlorophyll?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is located in the thylakoid membranes.

questions.text: Which evidence supports the endosymbiotic theory?

choices.label: They have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes
They are found only in animal cells
Chloroplasts have no membranes at all
Both organelles have linear DNA like the nucleus

questions.explanation: Having bacterial-type circular DNA and 70S ribosomes suggests mitochondria were once free-living bacteria.

takeaways: Mitochondria produce ATP via cellular respiration.
The cytoskeleton provides shape, support, and movement.
The endosymbiotic theory explains the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts.
